name: Earth Centre, Doncaster
text: Your train passes near the site of the Earth Centre, on the train's {side}, a visitor attraction about the environment and sustainable living, set out on 400 acres of a former colliery. It opened in 1999 with money from the Millennium Commission, the European Commission and English Partnerships, but closed in 2004.

name: Don Pottery
text: Your train passes near the site of the Don Pottery, on the train's {side}, founded in 1790 by John Green of the Leeds Pottery. The porcelain it made from 1810 to 1830 was of very high quality and was sold all over the world; the factory closed in 1893.

name: Rotherham Bridge
text: Your train passes near Rotherham Bridge, on the train's {side}, a stone bridge over the River Don begun around 1483. Its Chapel of Our Lady, built on the central pier, makes it one of only four medieval bridges in England with a bridge chapel still intact; after the Reformation the chapel served as a lock-up, known as the Bridge Gaol.

name: Rotherham Minster
text: Your train passes near Rotherham Minster, on the train's {side}, a Perpendicular Gothic church whose tall spire is the town's best-known landmark. Pevsner called it one of the largest and stateliest churches in Yorkshire; it was given minster status in 2004.

name: Tinsley Viaduct
text: Your train passes near Tinsley Viaduct, on the train's {side}, which carries the M1 and the A631 across the Don Valley on two decks, one above the other. Opened in 1968, it was the first two-tier road bridge in the United Kingdom.

name: Milton Ironworks
text: Your train passes near the site of the Milton Ironworks, on the train's {side}, run by the Dawes brothers and linked by a tramroad to the Dearne and Dove Canal. It closed in 1884, after a slump in the iron trade; the site is now a playing field, looked over by a pub called The Furnace.

name: Earl Fitzwilliam's private railway station
text: Your train passes near Earl Fitzwilliam's private railway station, on the train's {side}, opened in 1870 at the top of the Elsecar branch. The Earl's parties left from here for the St Leger races at Doncaster, after waiting in a drawing room upstairs; the building still stands, in the Elsecar Heritage Centre.

name: Oakwell
text: Your train passes near Oakwell, on the train's {side}, the home ground of Barnsley Football Club. It was the first stadium in English football to have a stand set aside for disabled supporters.

name: Old Queen's Head
text: Your train passes near the Old Queen's Head, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed building of the 15th century and the oldest surviving house in Sheffield. In 1582 it belonged to the Earl of Shrewsbury and was called the Hall i' th' Ponds; it became part of the pub next door after 1862.

name: Abbeydale Industrial Hamlet
text: Your train passes near Abbeydale Industrial Hamlet, on the train's {side}, a scythe-making works on the River Sheaf that ran until the 1930s and is now a museum. It is a remarkably complete 19th-century works, where most of the making was done on the one site, much like a modern factory.

name: Totley Tunnel
text: Your train runs through Totley Tunnel under Totley Moor, 6,230 yards long and finished by the Midland Railway in 1893. When it was completed it was the second-longest railway tunnel in the UK, after the Severn Tunnel.

name: Darnall Works
text: Your train passes near the Darnall Works, on the train's {side}, a steelworks that Sanderson Brothers took over in 1835 on the site of the Don Glass Works. It is the only large group of crucible furnaces still standing; some of its buildings are listed, and part of the site is a scheduled monument.

name: Darnall New Ground
text: Your train passes near the site of Darnall New Ground, on the train's {side}, an important cricket ground in the 1820s and the home of Sheffield Cricket Club. It took the place of the Darnall Old Ground, which the club had used in the early 1820s.

name: Gulliver's Valley
text: Your train passes near Gulliver's Valley, on the train's {side}, a theme park for families with children aged two to 13. Its opening was held up by the coronavirus pandemic, and it opened in July 2020, with sister parks at Warrington, Matlock Bath and Milton Keynes.

name: Norwood Tunnel
text: Your train passes near the eastern end of Norwood Tunnel, on the train's {side}, which took the Chesterfield Canal more than a mile through Norwood Hill. Begun under James Brindley in 1771 and opened in 1775, it was lined with three million bricks; it was closed when it collapsed in 1907.

name: Shireoaks Hall
text: Your train passes near Shireoaks Hall, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century country house built for Thomas Hewett between 1612 and 1617, probably by John Smythson. Its landscaped park is on the register of historic parks and gardens, and its formal water gardens, now separately owned, are a scheduled monument.

name: Church of St Andrew the Apostle, Bolton upon Dearne
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Andrew the Apostle, on the train's {side}, whose nave still has Anglo-Saxon stonework, with long-and-short quoins and narrow round-headed windows. The church was recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086.

name: Highgate Stadium
text: Your train passes near Highgate Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound track built on a site with railway lines all round it. It is an independent, or flapping, track, not affiliated to the sport's governing body, and was the subject of a BBC documentary in 2008.

name: Thurnscoe Hall
text: Your train passes near Thurnscoe Hall, on the train's {side}, a house of ashlar sandstone built between 1670 and 1701 for Thomas Shirecliff. When its last lord of the manor, Thornaby Taylor, died without an heir in 1926, the manor's line came to an end.

name: Hickleton Main Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Hickleton Main Colliery, on the train's {side}, a coal mine worked from 1892 to 1988. In 1933 it employed 2,560 people underground and 500 on the surface, and in 1944 King George VI and Queen Elizabeth came to thank its miners for their war work; the site is now Phoenix Park.

name: Old Vicarage, Church Fenton
text: Your train passes near the Old Vicarage, on the train's {side}, probably a 14th-century hall, partly rebuilt in the 16th, with a timber frame inside walls of magnesian limestone and brick. Thought unfit for a vicar from the middle of the 18th century, it was let to others, and in 1866 it was sold and made into three cottages.

name: St Wilfrid's Church, Scrooby
text: Your train passes near St Wilfrid's Church, Scrooby, on the train's {side}, built in the 15th century. William Brewster, one of the Pilgrim Fathers, worshipped here: the Separatist group at Scrooby fled to Holland in 1608, and in 1620 sailed to America on the Mayflower.

name: All Saints Church, Gainsborough
text: Your train passes near All Saints Church, Gainsborough, on the train's {side}, rebuilt between 1736 and 1744 to a design attributed to Francis Smith of Warwick. Only the 14th-century tower of the older church was kept.

name: All Saints' Church, Beckingham
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, Beckingham, on the train's {side}, which dates from the 13th century and was restored by Ewan Christian in 1892. Its organ was built in 1847.

name: Goddards
text: Your train passes near Goddards, on the train's {side}, an Arts and Crafts house built in 1927 for Noel and Kathleen Terry, of the Terry's chocolate family. It was the last major work of the York architect Walter Brierley; the National Trust has owned it since 1984, and its garden is open to visitors in season.

name: Abbot's Staith
text: Your train passes near Abbot's Staith, on the train's {side}, a stone warehouse built in about 1500, thought to have been the quay and timber yard of the monks of Selby Abbey. Since 2015 a local group has been raising money to restore it for community use.

name: Mansion House, Doncaster
text: Your train passes near the Mansion House, on the train's {side}, designed by James Paine and opened in 1749 as a place where the town's corporation could entertain. King Charles III conferred city status on Doncaster here in November 2022.

name: St Oswald's Church, Kirk Sandall
text: Your train passes near St Oswald's Church, on the train's {side}, now cared for by the Churches Conservation Trust. Most of it was built in the 12th century; its Rokeby Chapel is named after William Rokeby, rector here from 1487 to 1502, who went on to become Archbishop of Dublin.

name: Hatfield Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Hatfield Colliery, on the train's {side}, which mined coal, with a break from 2001 to 2007, from 1916 until June 2015. In 2013 a landslip of its spoil heap blocked this line, from Doncaster towards Scunthorpe and the Humber ports, for around six months.

name: Doncaster Greyhound Stadium
text: Your train passes near Doncaster Greyhound Stadium, on the train's {side}, made from marshland into a speedway track in 1929; the first speedway meeting was held on Easter Monday 1930. Greyhounds have raced here since a track for them and for whippets was added in 1941.

name: Siemens Goole
text: Your train passes near the Siemens train factory, on the train's {side}, opened in October 2024 to build new Tube trains for the Piccadilly line, part of a £1.5 billion order for 94 trains.

name: Timm's Mill
text: Your train passes near Timm's Mill, on the train's {side}, a tarred-brick windmill built around 1800. Edward Timm bought it in 1868 and his family's business ran the site until 2001; the steam flour mill beside it has gone, but the four-storey tower survives.

name: Snaith Priory
text: Your train passes near Snaith Priory, on the train's {side}, the parish church of St Laurence, which began around 1100 as a small cell of Selby Abbey, where two or three monks looked after the abbey's estates. Its building spans the Norman, Early English and Perpendicular styles.

name: St Paul's Church, Hensall
text: Your train passes near St Paul's Church, on the train's {side}, designed by William Butterfield for Viscount Downe and completed in 1854, in pinkish-red brick with a pyramid-roofed tower. Butterfield also designed the vicarage and the school beside it.

name: The Red House, Hensall
text: Your train passes near the Red House, on the train's {side}, built by William Butterfield in 1854 as the vicarage for the church next door. One historian has written that it could easily be mistaken for a house by Philip Webb, and that it challenges the Red House in Bexleyheath as the first conscious Victorian return to a plain, honest style of house.

name: Kellingley Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Kellingley Colliery, on the train's {side}, known as the Big K. Its shafts were sunk from 1960, through waterlogged ground frozen with brine, and its closure on 18 December 2015 marked the end of deep-pit coal mining in Britain.

name: All Saints' Church, Pontefract
text: Your train passes near All Saints' Church, on the train's {side}, a church of the 14th and 15th centuries left in ruins by the sieges of the English Civil War, when 60 cannonballs were fired at it in a single day. A smaller church was built within its ruined walls in the late 1960s.

name: Goole railway swing bridge
text: Your train crosses the River Ouse on the Goole railway swing bridge, designed by Thomas Elliot Harrison for the North Eastern Railway and opened in 1869. Its swing span, weighing 670 tons, could be turned to let ships through in 50 seconds.

name: RAF Bellasize
text: Your train passes near the site of RAF Bellasize, on the train's {side}, a grass airfield opened in 1916 for home defence squadrons. It was one of only four RAF sites in Yorkshire used in both world wars, though it often flooded, being so close to the River Ouse.
